content: This condition was notably prevalent among soldiers engaged in trench warfare during the winters of World War I, World War II, and the Vietnam War. Immersion foot develops when the feet remain cold and wet while being confined in tight or restrictive footwear. Unlike frostbite, immersion foot does not necessitate freezing temperatures and can manifest in environments with temperatures as high as 60°F (approximately 16°C). In the early stages, affected feet become numb and may exhibit discoloration, turning red or blue. As the condition progresses, swelling of the feet is commonly observed. In more advanced cases, the skin may develop blisters and open sores, which are highly susceptible to secondary fungal infections. This severe form of the condition is sometimes referred to as jungle rot. If left untreated, immersion foot can lead to tissue necrosis and gangrene, necessitating amputation in severe cases. When treated appropriately, full recovery from immersion foot is typically achievable. However, the recovery process is often accompanied by intense, short-term pain as sensation returns to the affected areas. It is important to note that individuals who have experienced immersion foot are at an increased risk of developing the condition again in the future. During World War I, British soldiers were instructed to carry multiple pairs of clean socks and to change them at least three times daily. Additionally, they were provided with whale grease to apply to their feet, which was intended to create a waterproof barrier. Regular foot inspections by officers were also implemented as a preventative strategy. The combination of cold, wet conditions and the inadequate waterproofing of the DMS boots contributed to a resurgence of the condition. A substantial number of soldiers were rendered unfit for duty due to immersion foot, and there were concerns that the British military advance might have been halted had the conflict not concluded when it did.
